The sentence pronounced upon these þÿ hv-> natives by the council of war of the division of Algiers was carried into effect on Saturday the 11th of April last. At half-past 11 the criminals were brought out ot prison. Before leaving it, Ben Mouktar, who prescrved all his cnogy, kissed the hands ol all the persons who surrounded him, natives and Frenchmen indifferently. When they arrived at the place of execution, beyond the gate of Bab Azoun, Ben Mouktar appeared surprised at the immense concourse of people who crowned the neighbouring heights, llis step was firm and bold ; the sight of the scaffold, surrounded by troops, caused him no emotion ; but the tottering steps of his accomplice betokened that his moral faculties were entirely gone. The Moorish public crier then cried out the following words in the Arabic language: þÿ "Inhabitants of the city, behold the fate of the male factors þÿ of those who attempt the lives of their fellow creatures, of those who assassinate Frenchmen ; know all who listen to me at. this awful moment, that he who treads the law of humanity under foot must expect a similar punishment." An officer then read the sentence, and Ben Mouktar first mounted the scaffold. When placed on his knees, he turned his head to examine the preparations of the executioner, and then uttered these words : þÿ " There is no God but Clod, and Mahomet is his prophet !" A single blow of a yataghan severed his head from his
body. Gileli did not manifest the same intrepidity, but was assisted to ascend the scaffold.

LEIStJRF.- Tho most fnlacious ideas prevail respecting leisure. People are always saying to themselves. " I would do this, and I would do that, if I had leisure." Now, there is no condition in which the chance of doing any good is less than in the condition of leisure. The man fully employed may he able to gratify his good dispositions by improving himself or his neighbours, or serv ing the public in some useful way ; but the man who has all his time to dispose of as he pleases, has but a poor chance, indeed of doing so. To do increases the capacity doing of ; and it is far less difficult for a man who is in a habitual course of exertion to exert himself a little more for an extra purpose, than for the man who does li'tle or nothing to put himself into motion for the same end. This is owing to a principle of our moral nature, which is called the vis inertias, litterallv, the strength of inactivity, but which I will explain at once to unlearned persons by reminding them, that to set a common child's hoop a-going in the first place requires a smarter stroke than to keep it in motion after wards. There is a reluctance in all things to he set a-going ; bat when that is got oven then every tiling goes sweetly enough. Just so is it with the idle man. In losing the halrit, he loses the power of doing. But a man who is busy about some regular employment for a proper length of time every day, can very eesily do something else during the remaining hours indeed, the recreation of the weary man

is apt to he busier than the perpetual leisure of the Idle. As ho walks through the world his hands hang unmuffled and ready by his side, and he can sometimes do more by a single touch in passing, than a vacant is likely to do in a twelvemonth. All this is exemplified fully in the actual practice of life. W ho, I would ask, compose the class w ho perform most of the business of public charity ? It is not those who are highly endowed with wealth and leisure. It is not in general those whom wealth has placed at ease, hut the class of well employed traders and manufacturers, who, to appearance, are entirely engrossed hv their own concerns. þÿ These men will snatch an occasional hour from their well employed lives þÿ perhaps an hour that ought to be devoted to relaxation þÿ and do you more real work in that time than an idle man would accomplish in halt of his yaw yaw existence. What is curious, if you place busy the trader on the shelf, as no longer requiring, to work for his subsistence, he immediately loses the power doing of these little superfluous acts of goodness. In getting out of the way of all exertion, he becomes unable to do any thing, even when he wishes it. On the same principle, men never gives a job to a lawyer oi any body else, who is not pretty well occupied. And this from no irrational homage to the name of the man, as is sometimes thought : it is because the man who does much is most likely to do more, and most likely to do it well Let no man then cry for leisure in order to

do any thing. Let him rather pray that ho may never have leisure If he really wishes to do any good thing, he will always find time for it, by properly arranging his other employments. The person who thus addresses the public has acquired the power of doing so, such as it is, not by having had a great denj of time at his own disposal, but solely by ravishing the inglorious hours w hich the most of

men spend in Unprofitable and onmymjed pleasures, and employing them in the cultivation of his mind. There is an nnec<!"' 'dd of a French author of distinction, who, by iegularly employing, in a few jottings, the wait minutes which his wife caused him to ii.e every last formed a book; certainly day while she dressed for dinner, least not the at meritorious of his works. Hazlitt also remarks, that many men walk as much idly upon Fall Mall in a few years, as would carry them round the globe. In fact, it may be said that to ask for leisure or time to do any ordinary thing, is equivalent to a confession that we are indifferent about doing it It is very fair that the busy man should he at case at last. It is often the object tor which he works. Neither can it be allowed that there is any absolute claim upon the wealthy to exert themselves for the good ol the community Wealth must he enjoyed as the possessor pleases, or it is no longer wealth, and one of the objects of industry is taken away. But. it would lie of vast importance þÿ both to the wealthv idle themselves and to the community þÿ it their tastes could oftener be directed to some beneficial employment within the range of their abilities and influence. It is a shame to those who are entirely at their own disposal, that almost all the general good that is done is done by those who are already overworked. It might rather be expected that the affluent, who have no particular business of their own to attend to, should devote

themselves to the general good. This is the more particularly to be expected when wo observe the worse than trifles upon which idle opulence generally employs itself. If actual vice he avoided, the mon contemptible frivolities and paltrv amusements are sought aftcr for the purpose of þÿ disgraceful word 1 þÿ kill' in g time. Sometimes we find the universal necessity of doing something, taking a good direction, or one at least rather on goodness' side. The female part of the affluent world arc often found to be actively benevolent ; and nothing can be more laudable. But the ells of idle humanity, that every day walk the street in vain, are beyond all þÿmensuration. Now, I am convinced that if these leisurely persons only once fell into the way employ- of ing themselves for some good end, they would find themselves far more comfortable than they are at present They would suddenly feel the inspiration of a worthy purpose of existence. They would feel the self-importance of active exertion þÿ the majesty of industry ; that lofty feeling which even the hard-work- 1ikj a housewife feels in increased proportion amic and a idst the which gives to the early riser right to slopcries of a washing his Saturday, taunt and look down upon all the recumbent part of mankind. The gentlemen must think of it They must up and be doing It is, 1 repeat, a disgrace them, in this universally to busy scene, to let all the laurels of charity and kindness be carried away by those who have enough to do to obtain their own subsistence.

Stammering and its Cure þÿ There is a. paper on this subject in the Medical Quarterly Review, translated from a for reign journal, which is, we presume, thought by our contemporary to he wot ih attention. This method of cure was, it appears, brought to Europe from America bv Mrs Leigh. She entered into partnership with a Doctor Malbouehe at Brussels, from whom the secret was bought by the Belgian Government : ti e system was likewise met with approbation in Prussia. The whole art consists in the following rules:-- The stammerer is to press tlio tipol Lis tongue, as hard as he can, against the upper row of þÿteeth is to draw a deep breath every six minutes, and is to keep perfect silence for three days, during which this pressing of the tongue, and the deep inspirations, arc to he continued without intermission. During night small rolls of linen are placed under the tongue, in order to give it the required direction even When three days have expired, the sleep during patient þÿ is to read aloud slowly to the physician for an hour. During this exercise, care is to be taken that the stammerer is never in w ant of breath, and lie must, therefore, he made to stop frequently and inspire deeply. The patient is to he admonished to keep the tip of the tongue floating when he speaks, and never to allow it to sink into tfie interior cavity of the lower jaw.

ROMANCE IN REAL LIFE. A few weeks ago a gentleman and a lady, elegantly dressed, the one three and-twenty, the other four-and-twenty years of age, drove up in a very handsome vehicle to the gates of the workhouse of one of the largest parishes in the county of Lancaster. The gentleman sent to the governor of the house, and requested to see him. The request was politely granted, and the lady and the gentleman were shown into the governor's private house. The parties informed him that they, were man and wife: that they had been married seven years, but that they had not been blessed with any offspring ; that they were very anxious to have an offspring, but that despairing of having any of their own they had formed the resolution of adopting a child. The governor was, as may readily be supposed, struck with the novelty as well as with the singularity of the object which had brought the lady and the gentleman to the workhouse. As, however, he saw no impropriety in the object, he complied with the request of the parties to be allowed fo inspect the infants in the house. Several were, accordingly brought for their inspection. After looking at several the lady fixed on an infant a few weeks old whose mother, a servant in the town, had got her bed in the house. So pleased was the lady with the child that she walked up and down the room with the infant at her breast, whose tender age, as well as its healthy appearance, strongly recommended it to her feelings. A dilficulty now, however, arose.

The infant's mother seemed unwilling to part with the child. Every eneeavour made to persuade her to allow the party to adopt the baby was unavailing. The result was, that the lady and the gentleman were forced to depart without having succeeded in their object. The negociation was again renewed, and again broken off owing to the unwillingness of the mother to part with her child. þÿ I hings remained in this state for a week, when, by the advice of her friends, the young woman consented to let the lady have the child, receiving a sum of money for the trans fer. The governor by direction of the overseers of the parish, now requested the gentleman to give him a reference as to his respectability. I he reference was given, and deemed perfectly satisfactory. The negociation for the transfer of the infant was then completed. The mother delivered her child to the lady, on a solemn assurance that it should be treated as if it were her own, but on the express condition that, though, on applying to the gentleman to whom reference hud been made as to tin: respectability of the parties, she should lie periodically informed of its health, she was neither to linow the name i or the residence of the parties. Such is a bra f account ot a very extraordinary instn.ee of adoption, and on the substantial accuracy of which our readers may rely, þÿ St. James's Chronicle.

THE ENGLISH LOVERS, AND THE DISCOVERY OF MADEIRA. To a shipwreck, according to the "Chronicle of Castile," the discovery of Madeira is owing. An Englishman named Robert n Mucham or Machin, happened to fall in love with an accomplished and beautiful woman named Anna d'Arfet, He was favoured with a return of her affection, but the attachment was contrary to the wishes of her friends who were of a superior rank to those of the lover, and seem to have possessed power enough to obtain his imprisonment. This was done with the double purpose of preventing the marriage of Ma chain with his mistress, and keeping him out of bet sight until a suitable match was arranged for the lady, and till hope extinguished by her marriage. The rites were solemnised, and the unhappy Anna

d' Ariel became tlio unwilling bride of some l/>nl, whose possession of her hand without her heart gave him the authority of a husband over a wife, or rather that of a master over a slave. Macham was now liberated, and soon after set off from the metropolis for Bristol, near where the husband of his Anna possessed a residence. The difficulty of an interview, which was no doubt enhanced by what had occurred previously to the marriage, was overcome by Mucham. Love always finds " out a way." The lovers had communication together, and an elopement was planed. Macham having, under some pretence, hired a vessel, he and his mistress embarked and set sail without their design being suspected. þÿ Tiie lovers had not long been at sea before a storm came on and their vessel was driven about by the winds and waves for thirteen days. The mariners knew not where the vessel then was, nor on what shore she might be driven. One morning about sun-rise they espied land, to the bearing of which they were total strangers. The ship made towards it, and as she approached the shoio several birds of a species unknown to those on board flew ofl" from the land, and fearlessly perched upon the rigging. The strange shore was the island of Madeira. The sailors now got out their boat, and making for the shore, landed upon the spot afterwards called Mechico> from Machin or Macham. A part of the crew was left on board to look after the ship. Upon landing they found a very fertile and beautiful country, richly diversified with hill

and dale, cooling streams poured down freshness and health from the hills in luxurious clearness, peculiarly grateful from the heat of the climate. A variety of trees covered with foliage of an unknown character overspread the face of the country, many of them bearing fruit. The turf w as enamelled with flow, rs of the sweetest odour, and the scene seemed to persons who had been so long tossed on a stormy soa, like an island of enchantment There grew a noble tree at a small distance inland which spread its branches far and wide around. Hard by the tree ran a rivulet of the most translucent water, the bottom of which displayed a bed of sand which set of its luui.spareney. They were so much charmed with the spot, that they erected themselves huts there with houghs of trees, and determined to sojourn in them for a short time. They had been on shore only three days when a tie pest arose and drove their vessel from her anchorage towards the coast of Africa, upon which she ultimately struck and was dashed to pieces. Those who were on board and escaped the waves were carried into a slavery w hich terminated only with life, by the ferocious Moors who inhabited that part of the Continent. When the storm had ceased, those who had gone on shore went down anxiously to the sea-side to look for tiie vessel, but it was no where to be seen. Despair was on every countenance hour after hour they vainly waited its approach, imagining it had been driven off the coast and might again re-

turn They expected it in vain ; abandoned upon an unknow n land, and without the means ot prolonging their existence but for a short pciiod, their spirits sunk within them. The constant Anna d'Arfet had lelt greatly depressed on leaving her native shores ; a presentiment of coming evil, w hich she could not shake off, was upon her mind, and this accident overwhelmed her with despair. The presages of evil in which she had indulged at

vssfEtxKKtast itaim&masma ' vwikulumkm -"> the commencement of the voyage seemed now to he fulfilled : her apprehensions overcame her, and soon proved too many for her strength; the shock of the vessel's disappearance, soon after she got the intelligence, deprived her of the power speech of She continued incapable of articulating a syllable until she expired, which was in the short period of three days after, the loss ot the vessel had been communicated to her. She was interred under the tree near which they find erected their lints, by her disconsolate lover and his followers. There are two statements respecting the late ol Mucham himself, one male s lain embark with his companions in the boat and reach Africa ; the other, arid that which is most commonly credited, gives him a grave on the island. It appears that he would not quit the spot where the remains of his mistress were interred. He would take no consolation from his followers, and he soon after died, tiie victim of his unavailing sorrow, requesting that his body might be laid in the grave of Anna d'Arfet, at the foot of the tree where they had taken up their abode. He was buried according to his desire, and a large cross of wood was erected over the ashes of the lover-discoverers of Madeira. The companions of Macham soon afterwards embarked in their boat, uncertain which way to steer, but encouraged by the vain hope of reaching England. They were carried at last by storms or currents upon the coast of Africa, where they were made slaves, as their com-

rades had been before them. There were at first lodged in prison, where, among other persons in a similar situation with themselves, they found a Spaniard named John de Morales. This person was an excellent seaman, and heard the narrative of the fate of Macham and his mistress with a lively interest, particularly as it involved the discovery of a new country, at that time an object of regard among maritime nations, and Spain particularly. Morales was soon afterwards redeemed from slavery, and returning home, was þÿ captuicd 011 the voyage by the Portuguese, to whom lie offered his services as a pilot. þÿ lie communicated to Prince Henry of Portugal tiie story of Macham; a vessel was immediately fitted out, and Morales entered on board in order to sail for the discovery of the new country. The command of the ship was given to Juan Gonsalvo Zarco, and much is related of the dangers and hazard of the voyage. They happened to touch in their way out at Puerto Santo, when they learned that to the north-cast, or more correctly the southwest of that place, a thick darkness was observed to bang over the sea, and rise up into the clouds, and that strange noises had been heard from the same quarter, but that none had dared to sail far from the land lor want of an astrolabe þÿ an instrument to steer by. Some thought the appearance was that over a bottomless gulf. Gonsalvo saw the same extraordinary sight, and partaking perhaps in the general fear, resolved to stay at Puerto

Santo until the next change of the moon þÿ John de Morales thought this appearance was nothing else but a sign of land, and bis energetic expression of opinion that it was so, alone prevented the further pursuit of the island in that direction from being dropped ; such were the superstitions of the age. The crew of the vessel were greatly frightened when Gonsalvo and Morales steered right onward towards the much dreaded object. As they approached the cloud, sornethingdense and dark was seen rising amid the gloom, which was the body of the Island. The seamen were scared with the appearance of

21% monstrous giants, to which tire: terrified senses changed tiie rocks scattered : ;<>ng the shore, seen through the mist. At lei gih the v sailed near a point of laud, which Gcrs-aivo called (Jape St Laurence. While passing by, the mist or cloud ascending, unveiled a good part of the sides ot the mountains, m d the ricli wooded landscape burst upon t' e view like a scene of magic. By aecidi lit they entered the V' rv bnv where the English ! d landed before them ; there they f'ounJ the tomb of the shipwrecked lovers, and Gonsalvo erected an altar on the sprit. He explored the island, and returned in safety to Lisaon.

With respect to feather beds, much difference of opinion exists, we believe the too common practice of sleeping in feather beds has a great tendency, to relax the nervous system, thus creating a susceptibility to disease. Persons anxious to keep the system in a healthv state should sleep on a mattress. The celebrated Mr. Abernethy used to state in his lectures that lie had never slept on a feather bed, and lie attributed his good health in a great degree to the habit of sleeping on a hard mattress Sir John Sinclair, in his 'Code of Health,' also states it as his opinion that the luxurious feather bed enervates tue system. We recollect an observation made to us by an officer who was engaged in the Peninsular war, viz. that lie never enjoyed such sound refreshing sleep, and such excellent health of bodv and cheerfulness oi mind, as when he slept for five or six nights successively on a hard floor. We might as well accustom ourselves to what arc considered as hardships, for we cannot tell in what situation we may be placed þÿ Oracle oj Health.

JERUSALEM AS IT IS. The general aspect of the environs of Jerusalem may be painted in a few words; mountains without shadow, earth without verdure, valleys without water, rocks without grandeur, a few blocks of grey stone piercing the cracked sand ground ! here and there a tig tree, and now aud then a gazelle or a jackall gliding fugitivcly among the broken rocks; a few wine plants crawling over the reddish grey cinder-looking soil ; at wide distances apart, little clumps of pale olive trees, casting a small spot of shade on the steep sides of a hill : the grey walls and towers of the city appealing afar otl on the summit of Sion this is the description ot the earth. 1 he sky is high, pure, clear, deep, and never does the smallest cloud float over it, or catch the purple colours of the evening or the morning. the Towards Arabia, a large gulf, dividing black hills, leads the eye to the glittering waves of the Red Sea, or to the violet horizon of the peaks of the mountains of þÿMoab. Not a breath cf wind murmurs among the dry branches of the olive trees ; no bird sings or cricket chirps in the herhless expanse ; a silence, eternal and complete, reigns in the city, on the roads, and over the country. Such appeared Jerusalem during the whole time we passed under its walls No sound was to be heard but the neighing of my horses, impatient under the ardour of the sun, or the melancholy chaunt of the muetzin, crying the hour from the top of the minarets, or the monotonous lamentations of 'I urkish mourners,

accompanying in long files, the dead ot the pest, to the different cemetries which environ its walls. Jerusalem, where the traveller goes to visit a sepulchre, is itself the tomb of the people : but a tomb without cypress, without inscriptions, without monuments : whose monumental stone is broken, and whose ashes seem to cover the earth which surrounds it with mourning, silence and sterility. We were seated one day opposite one ol the gates of the city. No sound arose from its palaces or its streets ; among the paths which wind as it were, at hazard among the rocks, were to be seen only a few Arabs, hall nakcd» mounted on their asses; a few camel-drivers from Damascus ; or some straggling women from Bethlehem or Jericho, carrying on their heads baskets of the grapes of Engeddi, or cages of doves, to be sold without the gates of the city, for the plague raged within. We went round the walls, and passed before al' gates þÿ no one entered þÿ no one came out þÿ even the beggar was not at his accustomed post No sentinel was to be seen at the barriers. We saw nothing þÿ we heard nothing ; the same void, the same silence reigned at the entrance of a city containing 30,000 souls» during twelve hours of the day, as there would be if we had passed before the gates of Pompier or Hcrculaneum. We saw only four funeral convoys issue in silence from the gate of Damascus, and a poor Christian carried out of the gate of Sion by four grave-diggers to the Greek burying þÿground. Lamartine.

REWARD OF HYPOCRISY. It is said that Constantius, the father of Constantine finding when he came to the throne, a considerable number of Christians in office, and at court, issued an edict requiring them to renounce Christianity, or quit their place. The far greater part of them readily

and resolutely gave up their employments and prospects in order to preserve a good conscience ; but a few cringed and renounced Christianity. When the emperor had thus made full proof of their disposition, he turned out every one who had complied, and took all the others in again, giving this as his reason for his conduct, that " those who would not be true to Christ would not be true to him."

the women of england. The women here are generally more handsome than in other places, sufficiently endow-

ed with natural beauties without the addition of adulterate sophistications. In an absolute woman, say the Italians, are required the parts of a Dutchwoman from the girdle downwards, of a Frenchwoman from the girdle to the shoulders, over which must be placed an English face. As their beauties, so alsot heir prerogatives are greater than any nation ; neither so servilely submissive as the French, nor so jealously guarded as the Italian ; but keeping so true a decorum, that, as England is termed the purgatory of servants and the hell of horses, so it is acknowledged the paradise of women ; and it is a common bye-word among the Italians, that if there were a bridge built across the narrow seas, all the women in Europe would run into England. For here they have the upper hand in the streets, tire upper place at the table, the third of the husbaudls estates, and their equal share of all lands þÿ privileges with which women of other nations are not acquainted. þÿ Peter ileijliris Cosmographie, 1052.

Exact lists of the town negroes together with increase or decrease are to be delivered to the commissioners. Jn like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 20th of September 1833 is to be attended to ; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with all the Inhabitants names without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much legularity as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the Royal westindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of Christiansteed and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils Incassator office and in Frederikstad and its Jurisdiction at the

police office in that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such in writing to the commission to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further directed, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof arc entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose to come forward with sutlicient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol. It is to be observed that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are made out according to the above mentioned schemes and every column properly filled up. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their houses, as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commissioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to be numbered and the name of the streets to be placed on both sides of the cornerhouses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor

General v. Cealsens placard of the 4th January 1777. lu case of non compliance with the above, the following fines arc to be paid and levied for: Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, be it either in town

or country, and proprietors giving in the lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beforemcntioned schemes will be subjected to the same fine, as the lists, in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect announcing themselves as such in writing arc liable to the same fine. 10 Ps. for every house number that is either wanted or illegible, and the same for every streets Name having the same defect. For all unpaid capitation tax under Ps. 20 a levy will be made within 24 hours after the time, when the lists ought to have been delivered to the commissioners. Furthermore all persons are requested to bring the exact amount of the capitation tax to be paid to each treasury, as the time will not allow to make change. The ordinance of 11th Nov. 1770, 10th July 1778, 13th April 1779, loth March 1792, nnd the 1st Oct. 1802, have together with the governor þÿgeneral placard s of the loth Nov- 1823, with the exception of the instalments for paying the capitation tax laid down the manner in which payment of taxes on properties in the. westindies arc to be paid, and the following rules are t<> be observed : I lie Negroes willfully not given up by their owners or by those persons in whose possession they are, will he sold for account ol the king, and the informer, if any. I he capitation tax to the royal treasury is 64sk. W. (J. for each town negro and Ps. 1

32sk. for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps. 1 for each town negro and Ps. 2 for each male negro in the country, to be paid thus: Capitation tax not amounting to Ps 20 immediately on taking up the list, but if Ps. 20 and above tha sum, in the manner specified in the ordinance of the 11th November 1770. That negroes born or dead in the course of the year, are not taxable, but they are notwithstanding to be regularly Specified in the lists delivered. þÿ All other negroes are taxable, including invalids. Exact lists of the town negroes together with increase or decrease are to be delivered to the commissioners. In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 26th of September 1833 is to be attended to ; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with all the Inhabitants names without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the Royal westindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of ChristiansUed and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils Incassator ollice and in Frederikstczd and its Jurisdiction at the

police ollice in that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such in writing to the commission to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further directed, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol. It is to be observed that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are made out according to the above mentioned schemes and every column properly filled up. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their houses, as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, writing in to the commissioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to he numbered and the name of the streets to be placed on both sides of the cornerhouses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor

General v. Clausens placard ol the 4th January 1777. In case of non compliance with the above, the following fines arc to be paid and levied for: Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, be it either in town

or country, and proprietors giving n the lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beforementioned schemes will be subjected to the same fine, as the lists, in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect announcing themselves as such in writing are liable to the same fine. 10 Ps. for every house number that is either wanted or illegible, nnd the same for every streets Name having tin same delect. For all unpaid capitation tax under Ps. 20 a levy will be made within 24 hours alter the time, when the lists ought to have been delivered to the commissioners. The French papers of Wednesday, which we have received by express, do not bring much news. Some of them state that Lord Eliot, who is said to be on his way to the north of Spain, on a mission to Don Carlos had an audience of the King on Tuesday. þÿ The object of his þÿLordship s mission is explained in a letter of our Paris correspondent, with whom, however we do not agree in the supposition that his Lordship had failed in reconciling the French Minister for Foreign Affairs to the interference of England in the settlement of the quarrel in Spain. It is as much the interest of France as it can be that of England, that civil war should be put an end to in the distracted provinces of the North of Spain. France indeed suffers more immediately hy the present state of things than we do; but though her Government mav entertain hut little hope that Lord Eliot will succeed in prevailing on Don Carlos to withdraw we are convinced that every thing has been done on its part to facilitate an object of such high importance to the interests of France. We find by the copious reports of the proceedings in the Chamber of Deputies which appear in the papers, that all the amendments proposed to the clause of the Ministerial Responsibility Bill concerning the right of action against public functionaries were rejected, and that clause, as remodified by the committee, and which renders a previous authorization by a Minister necessary before comment;-

in? an action against a public functionary, remains to be discussed. We also find in the Moniteur some news from the north of Spain, according to which the greater part of the 22,000 of the Queen's troops which were stationed about Pampeluna when Echarry Aranaz capitulated have been sent into the Borunda against Zumalacarregui. On their approach, the Carlist Chief divided his forces and marched in the direction of Esiella. A reinforcement of 8,000 men for the army of Mina has arrived in Navara. At Vittoria the arrival of the Minister of War was talked of. The Guide Nationals of Marseilles states, that some cases of plague had been observed in the lazaret at Leghorn. An official communication on the subject had been made to the Board of Health at Marseilles. þÿ Loening Mail.

I Tow to Sleep in Snow.þÿ The manner in which Capt. þÿBoss s crew preserved themselves after the shipwreck of their vessel was by digging a trench in the snow when night came on ; this trench was covered with canvas, and then with snow : the trench was made large enough to contain seven people? and there were three trenches, with one officer and six men in each. At evening the shipwrecked mariners got into bags made of double blanketing, which they tied round their necks, and thus prevented their feet from escaping into the snow while a sleep ; they then crept into the trenches and lay close together. The cold felt was generally 01 degrees below the freezing point of Fahrenheit, but in January, 1831, the mercury was 92 \ degrees below the freezing point. þÿ M. Alartin's Iiist Bri. C olonies.

On Wednesday morning last, the new Church in the Parish of Warwick, in these Islands was consecrated by the Right Reverend the Bishop of Nova þÿScotia. It was a very interesting scene. W e were highly pleased at witnessing the ceremony, which was simple, but impressive, solemn, hut free from superstition. Every part of the service was appropriate, and well performed We listened with peculiar gratification to the Sermon, which our excellent Bi-hop preached on the occasion from the second chapter ofllabakkuk, the 20th verse, þÿ " The Lord is in his Holy Temple, let all the earth keep silence before him." In the course of the Sermon after giving an animated account of the scriptural custom of setting apart particular places from profane and common use, and dedicating them solely to the worship of Almighty Coo, from the earliest ages, his Lordship eloquently adverted to the peculiar circumstances connected with the building of this Church, which now bears the name of St. Mary, lie praised the zeal of those members of the Establishment w ho had actively exerted themselves in its erection, and acknowledged in a very handsome manner, the liberality of the benevolent individuals, wh > though belonging to another communion, had kindly come forward to lend a helping hand to the goodly work. If our memory he not treacherous, the Venerable Archdeacon Spencer, had made similar acknowledgements in the Sermon which he delivered on the

opening of the Church The I'resbvt rians highly deserve these encomiums A more friendly and liberal set of Christians, we believe, can no where be found than the Members of this Communion in Bermuda. þÿ Serious they are, without being nnnecessai ily austere, and possessed of a dignity of sentiment, that gives no encouragement to the vcxatious system of proselytism. We sincerely hope that there may always exist between them and the members of the Church of England, the kindliest feelings of Christian concord þÿ Barbadian.

We copy from and Naval and Military Ga zette, of the 4th April the following notice of the services of Lieutenant-Colonel Mair, lately appointed Lieutenant-Governor of this Colony : .'The Lieutenant-Governor of Grenada. This officer, who has just received the Kings permission to accept and wear the ensignia of Knight Commander of the Tower and 8 word, presented to him for distinguished services in the field, is one of the few survivors of the original members, if we may so term them, of the 7th or Royal Fusileers, in which corps he has passed the greater part of his life Lieut, Colonel Mair was present at the siege of Copenhagen, at the capture of Martinique, and served throughout the campaigns in the Peninsula and France. He has been several times wounded, and particularly while commanding the storming party, the leading one to the great breach of Santa Trinidad, at Badajos, 6th April, 181:2, where he received a ball in tire instep, and where four officers of the five belonging to his party were killed. þÿ I ?ut. Colonel M. was on the staff in the ex pidition under Sir W Clinton, in 1826, to Portugal, and served with the Duke of Terceira's force while actively engaged lie was entrusted with a diplomatic mission to Greece : and, after his return home, employed previous to and during the special commission in 1830 and 1831, in forming a constabulary force throughout the Western part of Lngland. From 1831 to 1834, he was Military Secretary at Gibraltar.

Letter of George the Tiiird in Reproof of Routs. þÿ In the year 1772 the following letter was addressed by his Majesty to Archbishop Cornwallis. It will probably be new to most if not all our readers. " My good Lord Primate, þÿ I could not delay giving you the notification of the grief and concern with which my breast was affected at receiving authentic information, that routs have made their way into your palace. At the same time, I must signify to you my sentiments on this subject, which hold these levities and vain dissipations as utterly inexpedient, if not unlawful, to pass in a residence for many centuries devoted to Divine studies religious letirement, and the extensive exercise of charity and benevolence, I add, in a place v here so many of your predecessors have led th"ir lives in such sanctity, as has thrown I 1 .stre on the pure religion they professed and adorned. From the dissatisfaction with which yon must perceive, 1 behold these improprieties, not to speak in harsher terms, and on still more pious principles, I trust you will suppress them immediately, so that 1 may not have occasion to shew any further marks of my displeasure, or to interpose ia a different manner. May God take your Grace into his Almighty protection, 1 remain, my Lord Primate, your gracious Iriend, "C. R."

TO TIIE EDITOR OF TIIE MORNING CHRONICLE; Sir. þÿ An aristocratica! mouse of great in fiuenee in the political circles in which he moves, purposes from time to time, if agreeable, to contribute something in the w ay of information, touching the present Ministry, w hich all your emissaries, reporters, or correspondent, puttogether, could never furnish you with. I dwell, sir, well fed, and clothed in þÿnature s livery, perfectly at my ease, in Apslev house, the town residence of the immortal hero of Waterloo; and, consequently, there is not a mouse in this vast metropolis, that has a better opportunity of piying into the secrets of the State than your humble servant. Fearless of danger (for the eats of the Aristocracy are too lazy and well fed, to think ofhunting after mice), whenever the Duke of Well g-t-n is visited by the Premier, Sir Robert, or any other members of the Cabinet, I instantly creep forth from mv hole behind the wainscot, and listen with the greatest attention to their conversation. The result, sir. is what I purpose, as occasion serves, to forward to you for insertion in your highly popular and liberal journal I -hall date my despatches from Apslev house, which cannot fail to give my information, all over Europe, the highest political importance. Sometimes I may, instead of a Ministerial discussion, have to communicate to you one of the þÿDuke s s oliloquies; and 1 assure you, though Shakspean þÿ s, is bv far the better language, si ill those of Hamlet, Richard or Macbeth, are scarcely .

more appalling. Without farther introduction, 1 will therefore proceed to the point at once, and give you, as my commencing article, one of the most important and interesting ever submitted to public attention, which is neither more nor less than þÿ W ELI.IM þÿton P s RFAM. Apslev-honse, Jan. 10, 1835, þÿ Your Grace seems unusual! ngitnled this þÿmorning, observed the pre sent Eremin. Sir Robert Peel, on a late visit to the Duke of Wellington. þÿ I am. indeed. Sii Robert. A fearful dream lias tilled my soul with greater terror than all the batteries I ever þÿfaced. þÿ þÿ Really ! and they were not þÿmany, rejoined the wily Premier aside þÿ þÿ Your Grace ulai ms me, especially as, at the present very eritieal state of our affairs, owing to the unfortunate and unexpected result of the metropolitan and many of the provincial elections, every unt< ward event may lie regarded as an omen of our speedy downfall ; but if it be not soliciting too great a favour, perhaps your Grace would have the goodness to relate to me the dream which lias so terribly alarmed þÿyou. þÿ With pain, I will, Sir Robert þÿ for it W'ore impossible so to do with pleasure, even to oblige my dearest þÿfriend, replied the illustrious hero of Waterloo, bis blanced lips, quivering as he spoke ; þÿ but the dream, Sir Robert ; yes, you shall have the dream. Methought (commenced the Duke) my earthly career as soldier and as statesman being run. I was gathered to my fathers, passed the Styx, paid Charon his fare, and landed on the blissful shores of

Elysium. In the same boat, were some halfdozen shades of poor, ragged, Irish peasants, perforated hv musket-balls, they having recently been killed in an affray with the military. A Political Mouse in a Corner. Horrible Murder ut sea. þÿ The latest intelligence from India states that while the Young Rover, belonging to Messrs Cockerell &. Co. of Calcutta, was on her way from Moulmein to Bengal, two Manilla seacunnies, named Justo and Madrino, destroyed the vessel by fire, and murdered the Captain and several other persons It appeared that while one of the officers was sitting asleep on deck, Justo stubbed him iri the arm with a knife. He immediately threw himself down the hatchway and awakened the Captain. On the latter attempting to come on deck the two Manilla men threatened to kill him, and on his drawing back, apparently with the intention of arming himself, they closed the hatchway on him, the mate, and a Christian passenger. þÿ Justo then stabbed two Coolich merchants who were on deck, on which the Strang and all the Lascars flew to the rigging. The Manilla men then took the charge of the vessel, and ordered the Lascars down from the rigging to obey their orders, one of which was to fasten the stern windows. On the fol-

course would bring them to Rangoon, opened the hatches, and asked the Captain, on which the latter fired a pistol, loaded with two nails, but only a small charge of powder, and wounded Justo on the cheek and breast. Exasperated at this the two Mandla men determined to burn the vessel and destroy the Cap' tain. On the following day they collected combustahles and a quantity of tar, which they scattered about the deck and rigging and threw down the main hatch. They ordered out the jolly boat, making the crew and ll the whole table in a þÿroar passengers, amounting to 1(1, get into it; they then set lire to the vessel, in which were enclosed Captain Ewer, (the commander). Mr þÿH >do(the mate), and a native Christian passenger Having then gone into the bout them-

selves, they waited on their oars at a short distance from the vessel, till they saw it so nearly consumed as to leave no doubt of the three victims being burnt. The seacunnies then caused the Lascars to row for the shore, forcing seven persons overboard on their way, and stubbing and spearimr them to death when in the water. Not able to reach the shore from the swell of the sea, they returned and took from the wreck eight to ten viss of silver which had melted by the fire, there having been on board a lac and 40,000 rupees in specie. On proceeding towards Rangoon some of the Lascars told what had happened at a small village, when they were all taken into custody by a native magistrate, but the seacunnies escaped by bribing the officer who had efuirge of them. They were, however, afterwards apprehended, and confessed the whole. The British President (Colonel Burney) could not believe the story, as it was incredible that two men could awe so large a number, until the seacunnies informed him that the conduct of the captain had been so violent that all the men, with the exception of those destroyed, had entered into the conspiracy against him. The men are to be sent to Calcutta to be tried.

A Continental Wonder. þÿ The Belgian Journals contain the account of a case of somnambulism, or catalepsy, of a nature so extraordinary as to merit the attention of physiologists, and if the assertion of those medical men w ho have seen her be true, must shake the scepticism of the most incredulous. The patient is Sophie Laroche, a peasant girl of Virieu, in the French department of the Isere, aged fourteen ; and the most ridiculously romantic circumstances respecting her are offered to the gullibility of the public. þÿ Amongst others. Hr. Eytnard has published on account of his visit to her during the last month. This is not a place for entering into details ; suffice it to say, that the girl in question! in a complete state of somnambulism, with her eyes bandaged or in total darkness, can read and distinguish by scent, voice, and touch, persons near or at a distance ; that whilst labouring under the access, which lasts several hours, and sometimes davs she makes the most extraordinary revelations, discovers hidden and lost objects, find her way about the town, understands Greek, and Latin, penetrates þÿpeople t s houghts, and answers questions upon subjects which, during her natural state, she is wholly ignorant of. Her body, during some of these periods, appears to be endowed with a poculiar lightness and elasticity, so that she may be lifted up as though she only weighed a few ounces, or as if the mere approach of the hand served to render her buoyant. These, together with many

other marvels, are recounted by hundreds of persons who have attentively watched þÿher. It appears, however, that the accesses of catalepsy are gradually diminishing as she grows older, and that there is every prospect of their becoming totally extinct as her body gains strength. In the meantime, Sophie Laroche is the wonder and admiration of the whole department of the Isere, and has furnished fresh arguments for the speculations of the disciples of animal magnetism. English readers will only see in the statements respecting this girl, fresh instances of human credulity.

Cape of Good Hock. þÿ The advices yesterday from the Cape Good Hope arc to the of 12th February. They confirm the previous information of the successful operations of the military, and the Burgher forces, in expelling the Cadres from the colony. It is stated, that some time since, the Chiefs of the tribes beyond the frontier complained to the Colonial Government that hundreds of the colonists had invaded their country, and were laying in desolate. The reply was, that the Colonial Government did not approve of such conduct, but could not prevent it, as the jurisdiction of the courts did not extend beyond the boundary. This, it is asserted, was one of the principal causes which led to the incursion of the savages. The efforts of the troops in driving the Calfres into their own territory had been most successful, and with comparatively little loss of life. A party of troops and Burghers had pursued the Chief Eno and his followers, and completely destroyed them, Eno himself only escaping death by disguising himself in his þÿdaughter d s ress, while she put on her faþÿther karogs, s and received three shot wounds before her sex was discovered A Government notice had been issued detailing the movements of Colonel Somerset and Major Cox in clearing the colony of the Calfres, and confirming the adhesion of the Chiefs Pato, Cilms, and Kama to the colony The war was, in fact, at an end. þÿ Courier, April g8.

Extract of a letter from Salonica, dated 2d April : þÿ I beg leave to state, for the informaof the Committee for managing the A flairs of Lloyd's, the destruction of thirty-seven Greek pirates by the Turkish troops, of which thirty were taken in the vicinity of Cassandra, and the remainder in Thessaly. The heads of these malefactors were sent in here last week, and publicly exposed during three days. It is supposed that tins summary but necessary

act of justice may he the means of deterring other pirates from frequenting these parts for some time to come. For the capture of the | irates wc are exclusively indebted to our Governor, Ibrahim Pacha, who deserves unqualified praise for his conduct in tins instance. I am sorry to have to report the exisience of the plague here, introduced by a passenger recently arrived from Alexandria ; as yet we have only heard of four deaths out of seven attacks, and from the rigorous measures taken by the Consuls, with the consent of the Turkish Local Authorities, in subjecting the arrivals from Egypt to a strict quarantine, we hope that the disease may be checked in making further þÿprogress.

TREMENDOUS HAIL STORM. .Extract from the work recently published by the Harpers, from the pen ol Com. Porter, entitled þÿ Letters from Constantinople 15l YlCDUKli, Allg. 3. An event anxiously desired by our countrv, for some ten or twelve years or more, took place this morning, the exchange ot the ratification of the treaties between the United States and the Ottoman Porte. On our way from the residence of the minister to meet the Peis Eflendi, at Camlalie, halfway between this and Constantinople, and a few minutes after leaving the landing, I witnessed a scene the most awful and apal ling that the imagination can depict. 1 believe 1 have described what a kaiek is ; it is a boat in form like an egg shell, cut longitudinally, and almost as light and frail ; the passengers sit on the bottom of the big end of the shell, and the boat is rowed by three stout rowers, each working two short oars. 1 ht y are the lightest, the frailest, and the swiftest things that can be ; more easily capsized which demolished than an Indian bark canoe, and they very much resemble, except that they are highly ornamented by delicate carved work and gaudy gilding. In a six oared kaick, the American minister, his secretary, Ac. and mvselt, with his kervoss, or guard, a fine looking 1 urk in full costume, except the turban, (for the Sultan since the fall of the Janissaries, does not allow any one in his employ to wear the turban, nor does he wear it himself,) attaghan, pistols, and pipe, (pipe is a part of full dress) started with

the treaty and regalia of about thirty thousand dollars worth of snufl boxes, which you might have put in your coat pocket. We had got jierhaps a mile and a half on our way when a cloud rising in the west, gave indications of an approaching rain. In a few minutes we discovered something falling from the heavens with a heavy þÿsplash and <>! a whitish appearance. 1 could not conceive what it was, hut seeing some gulls I supposed it to be them darling for fish ; but soon alter discovered that they were large balls of ice falling. Immediately we heard a sound like rumbling thunder, or ten thousand carriages roiling furiously over the pavement. '1 he whole Bosphorus was in a foam, as though þÿheaven s artillery had been discharged upon us and our frail machine Uur fate seemed inevitable ; our umbrellas were raised to protect us ; the lumps of ice stripped them into ribbons. We fortunately bad a þÿbullock bide s in the boat, under w liicli we crawled and saved ourselves from further injury. One man. of the three oarsman, had his hand literally smashed ; and another was much injured in the shoulder; Mr. II. received a severe blow on the leg, my right hand was somewhat disabled, and all more or less injured. A smaller kaick accompanied, with two servants They were both disabled and arc Dow in bed with their wounds; the kaick was terribly bruised. It was the most awful and terrific scene that I ever witnessed, and God forbid that 1 should be ever exposed to such another. Balls of ice as large as my

two fists fell into the boat, and some of them came with such violence as certainly to have broken all arms or legs, had they struck in j those parts. One of them struck the blade of an oar and utes, but it was five minutes of split it. The scene lasted mav the be five min- most awful feeling that I ever experienced. When it passed over, we found the surrounding hills

tDiUTSX "OST2ST2>!f33t covered with masses of ice, I cannot call it hail ; the trees stripped ot their leaves and limbs, and every thing looking desolate. We proceeded on our course, however, and arrived at our destination drenched and awestruck. The ruin had not extended so tar as Gaiidalie, and it was difficult to make them comprehend the cause ol the nervous and agitated condition in which wc arrived ; the licis Etiendi asked me if 1 was ever so agitated when in action? 1 answered no ; for men I had something to excite me, and human means only to oppose. lie asked the minister if he was ever so affected in a gale ot wind at sea ? He answered no, lbr then he could exercise his skill to disarm or render harmless the element. He asked him why he should be so aflecled now ? He replied þÿ uoin the awful idea ol being crushed to death by the hand of God with stones lioni heaven, when resistance would be in vain, and where it would be impious to be þÿbrave. He clas pud liis liands, and raised bis eyes to .heaven and exclaimed, þÿ God is great ! Up to tins hour, late m the afternoon, I have not recovered my composure ; my nerves are so aliccted as scarcely to be able to in 'Id my pen, or communicate my ideas l lie scene was awful beyond desciiplion. all I liave witnessed repeated eai ihquakes ; the lightning has played, as it were, about my head ; Hie wind l oared, and die waves at one moment thrown me to the sky, and the next have sunk me into a deep abyss i have been in action, and seen death and desli action around me in

every shape ol honor, but i never before had the feeling oi awe winch seized u, on me on this occasion, and slid haunts, anu 1 reei vvui ever ha uni me. 1 returned to tiie beautiful v illage of Buvucdere. the sun was out in all us sj n nuor, at a distance all looked smiling and charming; but ncarct approach discoveievi roots covered vvitli woihinei) repairing die biokcn tiles; uesolated vineyards and sliaitcred windows. þÿ j My porter, the boldest of my family, who bad ventured an instant from the door, had been knocked down by a bail stone, and huu they not dragged him in by the heels, would have been battered to death. Ol a dock oi geese in trout of our house, six were killed and live dreadfully mangled. Two boatmen were killed in the upper part of the village, and 1 liave heard oi broken bones in abundance, j Many oi tfio thick brick tiles with which my j root is covered, are smashed to atoms, and my house w a> inundated by the rain that succeed- i cd this visitation It is impossible to convey an idea of what it was Imagine loyows f however, the heavens suddenly froze over, and as suddenly broken to pieces in irregular masses, of from half a pound to a pound weight, and precipitated to the earth. My own servants weighed several pieces of three quarters ot a pound, and many were found by others, of upwards of a pound. There were many which fell around the boat in which 1 was, that appeared to me to be as large as the swell ol large a sized water decanter. You may think this romantic. It is
as true as Gospel, and I refer you to Mr. , who will be bearer of this letter, who was with me and witnessed the scene, for the truth every of word it contains.

A sailor, finding the heat of the weather uncomfortable, determined to take a bath. He accordingly prepared himself, taking þÿoff bis shoes and outer garments, and binding up bis trousers in such a manner that they could not impede his motions. lie then commenced ascending the rigging of a brig lying at the wharf. He continued to climb up until be had reached an elevation, to dive from which was a feat so dc s pc rate that no one supposed he would venture it. Jack, however, looking down for a moment, said ho was not high enough, and recommenced < limbing. He at length attained the highest elevation, and standing on the round i lock that tops the highest mast, he balanced himself on his fearful perch, and prepared for bis desperate leap. A crowd had by this time collected, and Jack gratified his vanity by shouting forth w ith stentorian lungs, a speech. þÿ J\len, þÿI m going to dive from this here mast, and them vvliat thinks it a feat, ought to give me what they can spare, to encourage native talent, as the landsfolk say. þÿ So lie goes þÿI and he did go. He leaped from bis height head foremost down. A thrill and cry of horror ran through the crow d, as bis form darted through the air, and fell with a loud concussion, into the water. He was under the water but a short time, and rising on the surface and shaking the water from ins
hair, he re- lined to his vessel and ins vvoik. þÿ Fi.il. Ouz.

Our cotemporary of the West Indian, in his þÿyesterday number, s furnishes the public with a letter from Grenada, dated the 6th of this month, giving a particular detail of the injury sustained by the steamer Spitfire on her way hence to that island on the 3d instant þÿ which we copy for the information of our readers, in this impression.

( From the West Indian of yesterday ) Thank God ! news have reached us of the arrival of the Steamer Spitfire at Grenada, without the loss of any of the crew, or any human injury having been sustained. We have been most opportunely and politely favored with a letter, dated Grenada, 6th September, from an Officer of the Steamer Spitfire, giving a minute account of what that Vessel suffered from the commencement of the Storm, to her arrival in Grenada. þÿ We cannot do better than publish this valuable document verbatim : þÿ þÿ At 8, a. m., of the morning of the 3rd inst , the weather assumed a threatening appearance, with the wind from the N. E. H. M. Ship Champion, arrived with despatches for Captain Jones, and sailed about 8-45. þÿ At 9-30, the Commander ordered the fires to be lighted ; the sympthometer fell very fast and eventually eleven tenths. Several Mail- Boats slipped and stood out to sea At 10 30, the anchor came home ; at 1 1 a. m , slipped the cable and stood out to sea ; 11-15, the dingy þÿw as blown from the stern, and the gig swamped and washed from the davits þÿ the cutter stove and washed in board. The wind veered round to the southward and westward ; the sea breaking over the vessel ; hove the coals overboard that were lying on deck to case the vessel. 1, p. þÿm still blowing a hurricane, the main trysail, jib and forestavsail were blown from the bolt ropes ; ship labouring very much ; the foretrysail was blown from the gaskets; the maintrysail gaff carried

away. At 4, p m , the mainmast went below the deek, falling across the larboard quarter, without the slightest accident to any of the crew; the carpenter had gone forward for his axe, but before he returned the mast was bedded in the þÿship s s ide. The lining of the vessel was broke in several places by the violence of the sea. The centre hoiler became leaky, and the Engineers had to put out the fire, which impeded our progress had the other boilers sustained similai injury, we mu«t inevitably have been lost, as the seas were making a clean break over us ; we had all our hatches battened down, and still it required the exertions of the men to pump the water out. About 0, r. m., the weather moderated, and at 8, the night assumed a beautiful appearance, with a moderate breeze. Sometime before leaving Carlisle-Bay the spray from the sea flew so thick that we could not discern the length of the vessel. When we slipped we had three buinboat people on þÿboard Toby Blackman, Wm Carden, and Deborah Lopez who are now on shore at þÿ this place waiting a passage to Barbados. þÿ A Brig arrived this afternoon, and was off Barbados yesterday morning þÿ she experienced heavy squalls on the 3d, with the wind from the eastward, but nothing more she was then about 180 miles to the N. One ol the easiest, the most common, and the most periectly foolish things in the world þÿis to quarrel ; no matter with whom, u an woman, or child þÿ or upon what pretence, provocation, or occasion whatsoever. There is no kind of necessity in it, and no manner of use in it, and no degree of benefit to hi gained by it. And yet, stiange us the fue, maybe, theologians quarrel, and politicians quarrel, lawyers, doctors, and j iiulcis quarrel, the church quarrels, and the state quarrels ; nations, and tribes, and corporations þÿ men, women, and cliiidn n, dogs and rats, birds and beasts, quarrel about all manner of things, and on all manners ol occasions. Now that a great deal of mischief comes of this, every body secs, and ieels. and aun.os þÿ hut what good ; Many things, e\ il in themselves, have their redeeming n sul s. and produce at least their kernel ol wheat to the bushel ol cliall, hut il any bodv ever discovered a good thing come out of a quarrel, il þÿlie ll relations she may have made you ; neither to give us its length, breadth, quality, and description, þÿwe insure ll him a patent lor it. 1) there is any thing in the world that will make a man feel had, except pinching his lingers in the crack of a door, it is unquestionably a quarrel. No man ever fails to think less of j himself alter than he did before one, it degrades ; linn in his own eyes and in the eyes of others and what is worse, blunts his sensibility to disgrace <>n the one hand, and increases the

power of passionate irritability on the other. Some tilings look very well in theory, which nt answer at all in practice ; and it is possible for a man to reason himself into the belie!, that a particular si stem is right, which, , when reduced to practice, will turn out en- I tirely wrong. But neither the theory nor the j practice of quarrelling is good. The reason people quarrel about religion is, because they really have so little of it, and tlie harder they quarrel, the more abundantly do they prove it. A man has a right to stand fast by his religious þÿfaith a l ight to insist upon þÿil a right to present it respectfully on all proper occasions, to the consideration of others ; but lie lias no right to quarrel þÿ and any man that will quairel about these things, in my opinion, lias not much io quarrel about. Politicians need not quarrel. Whoever quarrels with a man for his political opinion, is himself dem ing the first principles of freedom þÿ freedom of thought þÿ moral liberty without which there is nothing in politics worth a þÿgroat it is therefore wrong upon principle. You have on this suby ct, a right to your own opinions þÿ so have others ; you have a right to convince them if you can they have the same. Exercise your rights, but again I say, þÿDon quarrel. t The truth is, the more quietly and peaceably we all get on, the þÿbelter the better for ourselves, the better for our neighbors. ( From the Barbados Mercury, Sept. 22 d 1835) A most daring and atrocious act of robbery was last night perpetrated by some person or persons unknown, who boarded and made off with a fine large fishing boat, the property of Mr. John W. King, a most industrious and deserving individual. Tfie boat, as usual, had been out in the day, and on her return from fishing, was anchored at her moorings in the channel, where she was left by her hands in the evening in perfect safety ; but this morning had disappeared, no one knows how, except upon the previous supposition that she has been stolen and carried to leeward, as her sails, rigging, Arc., were all on board at the time. This boat is a very serious loss to the owner, and as the most certain means of recovering her, and if possible bringing to punishment the robbers, we request the favor of our Cotemporaries of the press in all the sister islands, to give this shameful transaction all the publicity in their power. A very strange and unaccoutablc occur fence has been communicated to us yesterday, and although not positively detailed, yet it bears an appearance of plausibility sufficiently strong to entitle it to our belief. Early in the morning as two gentlemen were riding in the windward quarter, near about Stubbs Ksþÿtut they , perceived at a distance in the sea an object which arrested their attention, and which at first sight appeared to be the spouting of a whale, but from Its duration and perpendicular steadiness, they afterwards surmised to be a water spout þÿ riding on, however, and varying their conjectures according to the continuity of the phenomenon, as they apprehended it, with the surface of the water, they arrived at a situation affording a better view of its situation, and upon spying discovered it to be the remains of a vessel burnt down nearly to the þÿwater e s dge ; and which sunk almost directly after. Their observation was soon after corroborated by a few apprentices, who affirmed that they had early seen it, and believed it to be a schooner on fire.

Mormng Herald. þÿ We understand that all the South American States, which were formerly colonies of Spain, are to be forthwith recognised as independent by the ministers of the Queen. This is a measure which, though long delayed, is not now the less wise and just. The only wonder is that, with the example of England and her refractory children in the northern part of the same New World so long before his eyes, any Spanish statesman could indulge in the vain hope of reducing these for distant and extensive districts again to the dominion of his country. For years it has been apparent to every body, but the people of Madrid, that Paris was as likely to become the seat of a Spanish viceroy as Buenos Ayres and Mexico. Indeed theques tion of recognition affects the mother country now more than the colonies. The latter are, in fact, independent, and have been so generally recognised. They may look for some commercial benefits, but can derive no addition of political importance from a reunion with Spain, whilst to her trade this new field for extension cannot prove otherwise than advantageous. The ncgociation, to which a finish has, we are assured, been now put, was long and tedious. As in our own case with the United States, it was resisted by deeply rooted prejudices, which could neither be removed by reasoning nor conciliated. Had Ferdinand the Seventh still lived, nothing | would have induced him to assent to this act of recognition. The ministers of the Queen also coquetted, and affected to impose condi-

tions þÿ amongst others requiring some pecuni- j past. ary compensation for the concession, to which the South American agents would not for a moment listen. It is said of Cromwell, who was not a political appraiser, that he offered to sell the title of þÿ King of þÿFrance, with all its appurtenances, to the French for a few crowns ; but the French minister, who was still a better judge, did not think it worth a sous. So also appear to have thought the South American commissioners upon this oc- | south west. The sea were casion. Both parties eventually met upon equal terms, and no doubt the compact upon which they will agree will be mutually advantageous Already a passport has been expedited to his Excellency Senor Santa Maria, by the Spanish minister, as Minister of the Republic of Mexico dp. Senor Santa Maria will, we hear, leave London in a few days Madrid, put for to his hand, with that of the minister of Venezuela, already there, to the great and beneficient act of Spanish American independence and amity with the parent country. We wish we could compliment the states in question, now raised without any demur to the rank of nations upon their internal condition, as we may upon the triumph which they have obtained from without. But nothing can be more unsatisfactory than their situation þÿ almost one and all. Independence of foreign sway seems only to have cleared the stage for a struggle for power between a host of unprincipled persons, whose motives are any thing but patriotic. The provinces,
freed from the despotism of Spain, arc still groaning under selfish military chieftains, who have no object in harassing the country but thc gratification of their personal ambition. þÿ

BURNING OF THE SIR WALTER SCOTT. (From the Boston Transcript.) Captain Clark, of the Sir Walter Scott, arrived in this city on Sunday last, & proceeded yesterday morning to Boston. From his own lips we have received a full account of the burning of this gallant ship, an accident of a more extraordinary kind than has happened in the American seas for a long time

The Sir Walter Scott sailed from New Orleans on the 21st May, with a cargo of 1,794 bales of cotton, 18 seamen and 3 passengers, one of them a lady, Mrs. Hamilton, in a state of domestic solicitude. '1 he Ship was owned in Boston, was only two years old, and was valued at 22,000 dollars. Her destination was Liverpool. In coming down the Gulf Stream, this vessel encountered a heavy gale from the running mountain high. On the morning the 21st June, of about þÿo clock, in 8 lat 31 d. 24m. long. 75d. 43 m. when under double reefed topsails, and bearing upon the wind, opposite, or nearly so, to Charleston, South Carolina, a heavy peal of thunder broke over the ship. It seemed as if the heavens had been rent asunder. The captain and his three passengers were in their cabins. The lady started up in fright, and the enptain jumped on deck in so much haste as to be without his shoes. The electric fluid had struck the foremast, ran into the forecastle, where the seamen were at breakfast, dashed every thing into pieces, sent the men sprawling in all directions, and completely raked the vessel fore and aft, and between decks, and in the hold The suddenness and force of the terrible blow, made the vessel hang suspense for a moment on the top of in the billows. Every person was astonished, no one yet knew the extent of the injury.

þÿCrocodile E s ggs þÿ A rather ludicrous circumstance took place while I was on the shores of the Gambia, with some young crocodiles. A gentleman in England had written to his correspondent at Bathurst to send him some crocodile eggs : and, as they were plentiful in that river, they were procured and packed in a small cask with a quantity of sand. On the departure of the next vessel, however, they were forgotten, and were put in a corner till another conveyance presented itself. In the meanwhile the sun daily shot its powerful rays into the warehouse where they were deposited ; and one morning a tapping and rustling was heard which could not be accounted for. The owner of the warehouse assembled his servants, and, notwithstanding their reluctance, insisted on a search being made. Package after package was examined, without a step towards elucidation ; when, in a minute after a load had been taken from the top of the crocodile cask, the head of it was raised and split, and up came about a dozen young crocodiles. Thc negroes, who fancy the great origin of evil to be constantly near them, took this for such a positive proof of his vicinity, that they scampered off without ceremony, and left their master to face them alone. A short explanation induced them to return ; and the little monsters were destroyed as quickly as possible, their species being far too numerous in that river to admit of mercy to even one. þÿ We daily hear stories of the mischief crocodiles have committed ; and frequently sec

negroes who think themselves luckly to have escaped with the loss of a leg or an arm. A very fine Arab colt, belonging to the commandant ol Bathurst, was one evening led into the river to wash his legs, and as he came out again, a crocodile nearly bit off his foot above the fetlock ; he instantly (ell, and the reptile retired. The death of the colt seemed to be inevitable ; but, Colonel F summoned a Moor, who happened to be in the neighbourhood, and, by his judicious and skilful treatment, thc bones united, and the animal was saved. þÿ Mrs. Lee. þÿ Noble. Remedy for the Cancer. þÿ The T.ancet has a notice of a new remedy against cancer. It consists in the juice of a tree which the Indians employ to envenom their arrows; and it is also extensively employed by the hordes which inhabit the banks of the Orinoko as an anti carcinomatous remedy. Numerous experiments have proved that arsenic is neutralised by the secretion of a cancerous ulcer, while it preserves its poisonous properties when placed in contact with any other sore. The same phenomenon is observed with respect to the mancinella ; its poisonous efiects are in like manner neutralized hv the secretion of cancerous ulcers. The Indians, who employ this substance in the treatment of cancer, surround the wound with a pasty material, and then apply to the centre of the sore a few drops of the juice of the Mancinella ; an eschar soon forms, and coining away in about forty eight hours, leaves a clean wound, which rapidly heals. M. Germon, of Marseilles has witnessed a great number of cures effected by the application of this remedy, which he recommends to the attention of physicians.

A little after 5 in the morning of Thursday, taking our usual ride, the sky was lowering, the clouds flying about rather rapidly, (hi our return between six. & seven, we met with a hea\ y shower, and the wind was so powerlui it was with the greatest difficulty we carried our umbrella. From that hour we may sav the gale gradually increased, still blowing from the X. 1,., steady, but, to us, very alarming, with continual rain By half past ten it was decidedly a hurricane, and people generally made fast their doors and windows, and the merchants and shopkeepers closed their stores. The apprehension that the w iud would shift to the W of X., generally the most furious wind that blows in these latitudes, was uppermost in every nvnd. It continued however, steadily in the X E. quarter, until, we think, near noon, when it changed to S. E., or S. V E . and then blew | to with greatly increased violence. Alarm then became general, and the same dreadful results as we had so lately experienced in all their horrors, came vividly to our recollection. þÿ

The abatement of the storm was gradual, and people began open to their doors, and go out to enquire of the fate of their neighbours and friends.
