Margaret ! we never met before, And, Margaret, we may meet no more, What shall I say at parting ! Scarce half a moon had run her race Around this gay and giddy place Sweet smiles and blushes darting: Yet, from my soul, I frankly tell I cannot choose but wish the well.

I dare not wish thee store of wealth, A troop of friends, unfailing health, And freedom from affliction ; I dare not wish the beauty's prize. Carnation lips, and bright blue eyes, They look through tears, they breathe in sighs, Then hear my benediction þÿ Of these good gifts be thou possessed, Just in the measure God sees best.

But, little Magaret, may you be All that His eye delights to see. All that he loves and þÿblesses The Lord in darkness be your light, Your help in need, your shield in fight, Your health, your treasure, and your might, Your comfort in distresses, Your hope through every future breath. And your eternal joy in death !

THE TWENTY-EIGHT REGIMENT. (From the Glasgow Courier, Feb. 12.) The following account, historical and eulogistic, of the Twenty- Eight Regiment, was given by the Marquis Anglesey, of when pieaenting a stand ot colours to the regiment in 1834. It is extracted from a narrative of the campaigns of the regiment, by Lieut -Colonel Cadell, which has recently been published : þÿ " I cannot fix the exact period at which the 28th Regiment was raised, however, i find it engaged in the wars of Marlborough, and it served with that great Captain front 1701 to 1709 ; that it was much distinguished, and frequently noticed dispatches, in and thanked in orders. In 1759 I find it engaged with the immortal Wolfe. That excellent General þÿ that model of an officer w as killed at thc þÿ Storming of the lines of Quebec, whilst leading on the 28th Regiment. T he 28th were employed during the greater part of the subsequent American war upon that Continent, and maintained their high name. In the French Revolutionary war the 28th were also much employed. It became of great importance to reinforce his Royal Highness the Duke of York, then commanding the British and Hanoverian troops in Flanders. Earl Moira, since Marquis of Hastings, landed with his little army at Ostend, and by a skilful and rapid movement eluded the vigilance of the French army, purposely placed to intercept them, and successfully joined his Royal Highness. It was then ! first became acquainted with the 28th, and I soon began admire them. The 28th was to

severely engaged in the sortie at nimcgu' n. The French works were stormed, and their batteries destroyed. The position, however, of the armies made it necessary to retreat, and in this long retreat the 28th had arious opportunities of distinguishing itself, although no great battle was fought.

" Whatever were its difficulties, however it was harassed or distressed, it always turned out stronger than any other corps I appeal to the gallant General before me if this is not one of the most valuable qualities of a regiment. Hospitals were their aversion. Their home was their battalion, and they were never happy away from it. In those days the commissariat and the hospital establishment bad not arrived at that perfection they have since attained. þÿ It was commonly said by Commanding Officers that you might as well kill a man in the field as send him to a general hospital ; he was at least lost to the battalion lor the campaign. Not so the 28th. These poor ragged fellows (for they had lost their new clothing,) whatever had been their casualties, there were always crawling back to their home þÿ their battalion. You saw them in small groups, deserting, as it were, from the hospital, helping each other along þÿ halt naked indeed, but always bringing with them their arms, and in high order. '1 he locks were clean þÿ the bayonets were sharp. Finally, this regiment embarked for England. Their next exploit was the reduction of Minorca, under General Sir Charles Stewart þÿ Lieutenant Colonel Paget O always » at their head. They then went to Egypt. T he landing of the army on the 8th March, under General Sir Ralph Abercromby, was the most brilliant and imposing sight that ever was beheld it was gallantly opposed The 28th was one of the first regiments that formed on the beach.

They drove all before them þÿ cavalry, infantry, and guns. A position was taken upin advance. In it the army was furiously assailed at the dawn of the day, on the 2 1st of March. The 28th occupied an ancient ruin, with scarcely any cover in front, and entirely open on the flanks and rear. Having repulsed the first front attack of cavalry, they were again assailed in front, fianks, and rear. The simple order given was þÿ Rear ranks, about, fire !' Not a man gave way, and the enemy was totally repulsed. On this day the good, the gallant, the amiable Abercroinby tell þÿ regretted, deeply regretted, by all. Subsequently the army advanced upon Cairo, whicli they reduced, making 19,000 prisoners. Finally, the British army, having expelled the French from Egypt, was withdrawn from it. The 28th was next employed at the reduction of Copenhagen, and alter that formed part of an expedition to Sweuon under Sir John Moore. It returned to Portsmouth, and without disembarking was pushed on to Portugal, to reinforce the Duke of Wellington, then Sir A. Wellesly. It was not, however, in time to partake of the brilliant affair of Vitneira, and Koleia, which he achieved. The army then advanced, and took possession of Lisbon, and by a convention the French troops evacuated Portugal. General Sir J. Moore was now sent to command in that country. The 28th formed part of his army. It having been determined that an attempt should be made to relieve Spain, a corps under Sir David Baird was sent to Corunna, to advance

through the Gallicias, whilst Sir John Moore should move forward from Portugal. A junction was limned at Toro. Thc army advanced before Sahagun. A battle was to be fought; but General the Marquis de la Romana having announced the total inefficiency of his Spanish army, and his inability to second the efforts of Sir John Moore, it became necessary to fall back upon Corunna. Battle was offiered ai Lugo, but the enemy did not attack. The ret eat was continued. In front of Corunna a position was taken up, in which we were attacked. The enemy was beaten. þÿ A masterly movement ol General Paget with

thc reserve (the 28th of course belonged to it) mainly contributed to this result. He turned the left flank of the enemy, and they retreated. Here, in the presence of the regiment, thc brave, the favorite Moore fell ! here he was consigned to the grave ! The army embarked. In 1809 the 28th was of the expedition to Walcheren. Flushing was reduced. The same year it was sent again to Portugal, and a part of it was at the celebrated passage of the Douro (where General Paget lost his arm,) and at the taking of Oporto. Time will not admit of my entering into a detail of all the glorious exploits of the regiment in the Peninsula. Suffice it to say, that it bore very a conspicuous part in most of the great bat'les won there by the Duke of Wellington. It w as at Talavera, at Busaco, Torres Vedras, Albuera, Barossa, (the gallant achievement of General Lord Lvnedoch,) Arroyo del Melino, Almaraz, Vittoria, the several battles of the Pyrenees, the passage of the Nivelle, of the Nive, at Ortlies, at Toulouse. It closed the war at Waterloo. It had been closely engaged on the lfith of June at Quatre Brans, where it repulsed a furious attack of the French Cuirassiers. Though out the w hole of the 18th it was incessantly engaged at Waterloo Again, in its presence thc Gallant l'ieton fell ! " Twenty eight ! I have now brought you to the close of your glorious war. Glorious, indeed, and truly fortunate it has been. It would seem as if you had been predestined to form a guard of honour to our illustrious slain.

Wolfe was killed at your head þÿ Abercrombic died in your presence þÿ Moore fell by your side þÿ you witnessed the death of the Gallant Picton, who had so often led you to victory i "Twenty-eight! You began your career under the incomparable Marlborough ! Y<>u have finished the war under the immortal Wellington! 1 consign your colours to your charge. I do it in the most perfect, confidence. Whatever may be your destination þÿ in whatever cliine or country you may serve, I know you will bear them to honor and to glory. þÿ T wenty -eight ! May success ever attend j ou!"

Crows in Cf.yi.on. I breakfasted at the fort with Lieut. Dalgetty, part of which meal we were nearly deprived of, by a crow that flew in at the window; but it was fortunately saved by the timely entrance of a servant. These birds are so audacious, that all persons who desire to be secure from their marauding incursions must be very careful neither to leave doors nor windows open unwatched. When the natives are carrying home baskets of provisions on their heads, they are frequently attacked by a flock of these voracious birds who pounce upon thc contents : nor w ill they desist from the work of aboliation until the basket i set down, and they are literally driven away by the force of arms These bold thieves plunder children still more mercilessly, actually snatching the food from their hands ; and it is amusing to witness the art they use to dispossess a dog of a bone. No sooner has thc animal laid himself down to enjoy his meal at leisure, than a predatory covey descend and hoder over him : once more daring than the rest then alights beside him with the most unwelcome familiarity. The dog, startled and annoyed, suspends his labours, and growls out his displeasure, but, in vain, the crow advances with the self-possession of an invited guest ; until, at last, the exasperated owner of the prize lets fall his bone, shews his teeth, and makes an indignant snap at the pertinacious intruder, who dexterously eludes the bite which he has so cunningly provoked, while, at the instant the dog's attention is diverted, another
crow, who has been vigilantly watching the opportunity, seizes the coveted treasure, and bears it oil in triumph !" þÿ Ho/man.

From Chambers's Edinburgh Journal) In buying a horse, one of the chief requisites to be attended to, is the degree of nervous energy which the animal possesses; and it is the union of this energy with good conformation that makes many horses invaluable. Its absence or presence, however, is not likely to be discovered by the purchaser without a trial; and to avoid disappointment in this respect, it is therefore advisable to obtain one prior to purchase. The horse should be set to the work he will be called on to perfoim and if he is intended for the saddle fir single harness, he should have no companion on his trial, for many horses work well in company, that are downright sluggards when alone Some horses have an unpleasant way of going or are difficult to manage, or have some vice which is only displayed at work '1 hese arc so many more reasons for having a trial prior to striking a bargain. Rut it that cannot be obtained, some sort of conclusion regarding the animal's spirit may he drawn from his general appearance The way he carries his head, his attention to surrounding objects, his gait, and the lively motion of bis ears, may all or each be looked to as indicative of "bottom"' or, willingness to work. It is only, however, in a private stable, or in that of a respectable dealer, that these criteria can be depended upon ; for, in a market place, the animal is too much excited by the cracking of whips, anil the too frequent application of them, to he judged of as regards his tem-

per Neither must the buyer he thrown otl' bis guard by tint animation which horses display at an auction, or on coming out of the stable of a petty dealer, for it is a fact which cannot be too well made known, that there are many unprincipled dealers, who make it their business, before showing a horse, "put Some life in him," that is, they torture him with the lash, till, between pain and fear, die poor animal is so much excited as to bound from side to side with his utmost agility, at tlx; least sound or movement ol the bj slanders. The head, as being a part not at all contributing to progression, should, in tire saddlehorse, he small, that it may be light þÿ the nostrils expanded to admit plenty ol' aii, and the space between the branches of the lower jaw, called the channel, should he wide, that there may be plenty of room for the head of the wine pipe. In the draught- horse, a heavy head is not, as far as utility is concerned, an objection, for it enables him to throw some weight into the collar; and liejice, excepting its ugliness, it is rather an advantage if be is used entirely for draught. Rut it makes the saddle-horse bear heavy on the hand of the rider, makes him liable to stumble, and, wlu n placed at the end of a long neck is apt to wear out the fore feet and legs by its great weight. The neck of the saddle-horse should be thin, not too much arched, and rather short than long, for the same reason that the head should be light: and, in the draught horse it

In the ass and mule, the withers are very low, and the shoulders very flat, and this is the reason why they are so unpleasant to ride, and why it is next to impossible to keep the saddle in its proper place without the aid of a crupper. þÿ High Witlie rs, however, are not essential to the racer, or the draught-horse. The former does all his work by leaps, and that is performed best when the horse stands somewhat higher behind than before; neither .are high withers necessary to the draught-horse ; but in the roadster they are as important as the safety of the rider is, for a horse with a low forehand is easily thrown on his knees. In the draught-horse, this tendency towards the ground is obviated by the support the collar atlbrds. The chest should be deep and wide in all horses, but especially so in one intended for quick work, in order that there may be plenty

PFR'JONAr. AVE DOTE OF BURNS. ( F om 1,+sfh HunCi .on don Journal ) The fifth volume of Mr Cunningham's edition, one of the most interesting of the series, contains the poet's correspondence with the original publisher of his songs. It makes us feel no end of our admiration of Burn's disinterested love of his art, and his most gentlemanly patience with the publisher's criticisms. " Laddie, lie near me," (says he in one of his letters, speaking of a song), " must lie near me for some time. I do not know the air ; and until I am complete master of a tune, in my own singing (such as it is), I can never compose for it. My way is ; I consider the poetic sentiment correspondent to my idea of the musical expression ; then choose my theme; begin one stanza þÿ when that is composed, which is generally the most difficult part of the business, I walk out, sit down now and then, look out for objects in nature round me that are in unison or harmony with the cogitations my fancy, and workings of my of bosom: humming now and then the air, with the verses I have framed. When I feel my muse beginning to jade, I retire to the solitary fireside of my study, and there commit my effusions to paper ; swinging, at intervals, on the hind legs of mv elbow-chair, bv wav of calling forth my own critical strictures, as my pen goes 011, Seriously, this, at home, is almost invariably my way. What cursed egotism." It was modest in the poet to say that this was " egotism ;" but how truly the reader

feels that it was no such thing, and how glad we should have been of more friendly communications of the same sort. " Dumfries is a small town ; a few steps carried Burns to green lanes, daisied braesides, and quiet stream banks Men returning from labour were sure to meet him ' all under the light of the Moon,' sauntering forth as if he had no aim: his hands behind his back, his hat turned up a little behind bv the shortness of his neck, and noting all, yet seeming to note nothing Yet those who got near without being seen, might hear him humming some old Scottish air, and fitting verses to it." litis is a capital portrait in action. The homely touch of the hat turned up behind by the shortness of the neck, let us at once into the robustness of the poet's frame, and his freedom from coxcombry.

At all events, till we are shown to be wrong in the opinion, we must act upon it in what we have to date and to state on these points, and, accordingly, (to begin with a pleasant name), instead of making Ovid to have been born on the 20th of March, we put his nativity twelve days forward, and make a welcome gift of him to. April 1st. þÿ Ovid Born So that the April Fools have not all the days to themselves. þÿ His birth dates forty-three years before the Christian era at Salmo, now Salmone in the modern Neapolitan territory of Abrazzo. He was the son of a Roman knight, had an easy fortune, and (to use a modern phrase) was one of the gayest and most popular men about town in Rome for nearly thirty years ; till, owing to some mysterious offence given to the court of Augustus, which still forms one of the puzzles of biography, he was suddenly torn from house and home, without the least previous intimation, & in the middle of the night, and sent to a remote and wintry place of exile on the banks of the Danube. Ovid was a good natured man, tall and slender, with more aifections than the levity of his poetical gallantry might lead us to suppose. His gallantries are worth little, and have little effect ; but his metamorphoses are a storehouse of beautiful Greek pictures, and tend to keep alive in grown people the feelings of their
boyhood. A health to Ovid, readers ! for immortal men never die. We must speak of them as they still exist among us, and uot of their memories.

dr. vanderkemp. The Rev'd. J. Campbell says, Dr. Vanderkemp and his family had been taking a pleasure sail in a small boat one line summer evening, when a water-spout breaking near them, the boat sunk, and iiis family perished, while by clinging to the side of the boat when it rose to the surface of the water with its keel Uppermost, he was mercifully saved. Returning to his desolate home, he looked around all the fields of infidelity to find some Comfort on so trying and distressing an occasion ; but he looked in vain ; none of them yielded the fruit he wanted, all was sterility and desolation. At length he took hold of his long-despised and neglected New Testament, and pored over its contents ; when it introduced him to that surprising fact, which has been, and ever will be, the wonder of enlightened men, God manifest in the flesh in the person of Jesus Christ, and laying down his lite which he had taken into a mysterious union to himself, that he might redeem from all iniquity, and from all its merited consequences, a multitude of human beings, which none shall ever be able to number. He was led to see in this wonderful transaction what drew forth all the affections of his soul, and immediately cheered his disconsolate heart. He sat astonished, sometimes surveying, with the mind's eye, the everlasting misery from which he had escaped through faith in the great atonement for sin, made by the Son of God ; At then directing his eye to the ineffable delights, the pleasures of heavenly blessedness, to the hope of
which he had been raised through the same faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. He then thought what he should render some return

The Missionary Society had been formed only a short time before his conversation, and had attracted considerable attention on the Continent : to that society he offered his services, on condition that his destination should be to the Hottentots at the Cape of Good Hope. Captain Don Pedro Gibert, and Juan Montenegro, Manuel Castillo, Angel Garcia, and Manuel Bovga, were yesterday morning summoned to prepare for their immediate execution, agreeably to their sentence, for having, while belonging to the schooner I'anda, committed piracy, by robbing the brig Mexican, of !Salem of 20,000 8, and afterwards attempting to destroy the crew and all evidence of their crime, by setting fire to the vessel. It is understood that when the prisoners bee nne thoroughly convinced that there was no longer anv ground to hope for a further respite, they entered into a mutual agreement to commit suicide on Wednesday night. Angel Garcia made the first attempt, in the evening, by trving to open the veins in each arm, with a fragment of a bottle, but was discovered before he could effect his purpose, and a stricter guard was afterwards maintained upon all of them during the remainder of the night, and every thing removed with which they might be supposed to renew any attempt on their o.vn lives. Yesterday morning, however, about 9 o'clock, while the avenues of the jail resounded with the heavy steps of a host of acting marshals, and the busy note of pre- " p .ration" struck solemnly upon the ears of the spectators within reach of its echo, Boyga succeeded in infflicting a deep gash on the left side of his neck, with a piece of tin. The officer's eye had btcn withdrawn from him

scarcely a minute, before he was discovered lying on his pallet, with a peculiar trembling of his knees, which induced the officers to examine if any thing had suddenly happened to him. They found him covered with blood, and nearly insensible ; medical aid was at hand, and the wound was immediately sowed up, but Boyga, who had fainted from loss of blood, never revived again. Two Catholic clergymen, the Bev. Mr. Varella, a Spanish gentleman, and pastor of the Spanish congregation, at New York, and the Bev. Mr. Curtin, of this citv, were in close attendance upon the prisoners during the whole morning; and at a quarter past ten, under the escort of the Marshal and his deputies, accompanied them to the gallows, erected on an insulated angle of land in the rear of the jail. When the procession arrived at the foot of the ladder, leading up to the platform of the gallows, the Bev. Mr. þÿ ly at ('apt. Gibert, said Spanniards, ascend Varella looking direct- " to heaven" Gibert mounted with a quick step, and was followed by his comrades at a more moderate pace, but without the least perceptible indication of hesitancy, Boyga, unconscious of his situation and destiny, was carried up in a chair, and seated beneath the rope prepared for him. Gibert, Montenegro, Garcia, and Castillo all smiled subduedly as they took their appointed stations on the platform. Judging only from Gibcrt's air, carriage, and unembarrassed eye, as he glanced at the surrounding multitude, and surveyed the mechanism of his shameful death, he

might have well been mistaken for an officer in attendance, instead of one of the doomed. With the exception of repeating his prayers after the clergyman, he spoke but little. Soon after he ascertained his position on the stage, he left it, and passing over to the spot where the apparently lifeless Boyga was seated on the chair, he bent over his shoulder and kissed

him very affectionately. He then resumed his station, but occasionally turned round to Mr. Peyton the interpreter, and the clergymen. Addressing bis followers, he þÿsaid " Boys, we are going to die ; but let us be firm, for we are innocent." To Mr. Peyton, removing his linen collar, and handing it to him, he þÿsaid This is all 1 have to part with þÿ take it as a keepsake. 1 die innocent but I'll die like a noble Spaniard. Good bye, brother we die in the hope of meeting you in heaven." Montenegro and Garcia, though exhibiting no terror, vociferated their innocence, exclaiming þÿ " Americans we are not culpable þÿ we are innocent ; but we forgive all who have injured us" Castillo addressed himself to an individual, whom he recognized in the front rank of the officers below the see you in heaven þÿ sta«'e. and said þÿ . " Adieu my friend þÿ 1 do not care so mucn I I shall about dying, as to have the Americans think I am guilty," culpable. All ol them expressed great satisfaction at the intelligence of De Soto's reprieve. The Marshal having read the warrant for their execution, and stated that De Soto was respited for 60 days, and Buiz for JO, the ropes were adjusted round the necks of the prisoners, and a slight hectic flush spread over the countenance of each ; but not an eye quailed, nor a limb trimbled, nor a muscle quivered. As the cap was about to be drawn over Gibert's face, the Spanish Priest fervently embraced him, and during the operation of covering the faces of the others, the Bcv. Mr.

Curtin advanced to the railing of the stage, and read a brief declaration on behalf of the prisoners, addressed to the citizens of America assembled, setting forth, that as on the trial they bad declared their innocence, so did they now continue to do so. Bovga's cap and rope was adjusted, as he sat, supported by an officer, in the chair, which was so placed as to fall with the drop. At a quarter before 11, after every preparation was completed, and while they ware repeating to themselves, in scarcely audible tones, their prayers, Dep. Marshal Bass suddenly cut the small cord, which restrained the spring, and the platform fell w ithout even the creaking of a hinge. In falling Bovga's chair struck against the dodies of the Captain and Garcia. Boyga struggled slinhtlv once after his descent, and Montene- O gro and Castillo but little ; Captain G. did not die quite so easily, the rope being placed behind his neck. Garcia struggled most and longest þÿ about I! minutes. After being suspended 30 minutes, the physicians in attendance pronounced them dead, and tliey were cut down, and placed in black collins, in readiness in the yard. Alter the execution was over, Buiz, confined in his cell, attracted considerable attention, by bis maniac shouts anu singing. At one time, holding up a piece of blanket, stained with Bovga's blood, he gave utterance to his ravings in a " sort of recitative, the burden of which was þÿ This is the red flag my companions died under." The crowd assembled on this occasion ; is

estimated at from 20,090 to 30,000, and occupied every point that afforded the least opportunity fur witnessing the execution. The Spanish Consul having requested that the bodies might not be given to the faculty, they were interred last night under the personal direction of Marshal Sibley, in the Catholic burial-ground at Charlestown.
